item.title: Trapped fermions frustrate multiterminal Josephson networks
item.description:
Pay dirt theory — Trapped odd-parity fermions in multiterminal Josephson networks induce discrete vortex chiralities that suppress 2e order and produce algebraically decaying composite 6e phase correlations below a BKT temperature kBTBKT0/J=π3/72≃0.0756. In a two-trijunction device, the third harmonic of the free energy dominates below kBT×/J≈0.111.

Grade 0.462 · 2.3σ above the day's baseline · matched “Semiconductor spin qubits” · Antonio Manesco, Karsten Flensberg

Figure

Free energy (b) and its first and third Fourier harmonics A1,A3 (c) as a function of phase bias δ and temperature T/J. Shows the transition from a threefold periodic 6e potential to a conventional cosine 2e potential crossing at kBT×/J≈0.111.

Asks

How can microscopic fermionic parity and spin states in quantum-dot Josephson junctions engineer collective phase order and entanglement in a superconducting network?

But

Neglects higher harmonics of the odd-parity junction EPR, interdot cotunneling, and self-inductance; classical phase regime assumes island charging energy EC≪J; weak Gaussian bond disorder treated perturbatively.

Tools

XY Kagome antiferromagnet mapping · harmonic approximation with Green functions · exact diagonalization in truncated charge basis

Abstract

Coherent control of fermions has become a standard approach for engineering quantum devices. Here, we explore parity-induced frustration in multiterminal Josephson arrays. We focus on odd-parity Josephson trijunctions, where the presence of a trapped fermion induces a phase winding in each trijunction. Connecting these trijunctions constrains their shared phases, resulting in a long-distance phase coherence where the frustrated configurations dominate the low-energy physics. In the classical regime, these arrays map onto the Kagome XY antiferromagnet, whose established Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless (BKT) transition yields algebraically decaying 6e phase correlations. We show that the 6e phase coherence is manifested as a pronounced third harmonic in the current-phase relation of these arrays. While quantum phase fluctuations suppress the 6e coherence, we show that through spin-orbit coupling they also lead to spin correlations and entanglement between the trapped fermions. Our results establish fermion-induced frustration as a route to composite superconducting coherence and phase-mediated spin entanglement in superconductor-semiconductor artificial quantum materials.

item.title: Topological Quantum Reservoir Computing
item.description:
Worth a look theory — In a Kitaev-chain quantum reservoir, protected Majorana edge modes yield retention scaling as τe∼eN/ξ, balanced by local write-read residue ℛloc∼τe−2. Interactions (U≠0) autonomously load bulk memory into edge parities via second-order Liouvillian coupling at the expense of retention.

Grade 0.439 · 2.0σ above the day's baseline · matched “Quantum computation with quantum dots” · Zhi-Lei Zhang, Lianxiang Cui, C. P. Sun, Kohei Nakajima, Kazuyuki Aihara

Figure

Bulk-to-edge loading W and edge retention S across chemical potential μ/t and interaction U/t, accompanied by delayed-input memory function and temporal integration test R2 showing performance gains from including the endpoint parity Pend at long timescales τtar.

Asks

Can a physical system hosting protected topological information perform reservoir computation via its bulk dynamics while retaining processed information in its protected boundary modes?

But

Numerical reservoir task simulations performed at N=10, Δ=t, and tτ=1.5; analytic linear reservoir description strictly requires U=0; requires ensemble-averaged readout without mid-circuit back action.

Tools

One-dimensional Kitaev chain model · Majorana covariance space formulation · Liouvillian Dyson expansion · Echo-state property analysis

Abstract

Scaling universal quantum computation and implementing quantum machine learning with protected logical qubits remain challenging. To harness the computational potential of existing fault-tolerant quantum platforms, we introduce topological quantum reservoir computing, a novel approach using protected degrees of freedom for storage and the host system's intrinsic dynamics for information processing. Using a one-dimensional Kitaev chain, we show how long-lived Majorana edge modes and fast bulk responses support these complementary functions within the same many-body system. We identify the tradeoffs governing access to protected memory and show how matched interfaces enable programmable writing and interactions enable autonomous information consolidation from the bulk to the edge. These mechanisms improve performance on tasks requiring long-term retention of temporal information. Our results establish topology as a new resource for quantum reservoir computing and open a route toward near-term quantum computing and quantum machine learning.

item.title: Fe²⁺:forsterite Qubit System
item.description:
Worth a look new result — Simulated X and Z logic gates achieve >99.7% fidelity at 1.15 ns gate times in Fe2+:forsterite at temperatures up to 10 K. Natural tunnel splitting is Δ=0.19 K (4.040 GHz) under zero field.

Grade 0.426 · 1.8σ above the day's baseline · matched “Semiconductor spin qubits” · Dishaanth S. Pillai, G. M. Wysin

Figure

Gate infidelity of X and Z gates as a function of decoherence rate at T=10 K, showing infidelity remains below 10−3 at predicted direct-process relaxation rates.

Asks

Can the intrinsic zero-field splitting of a non-Kramers Fe2+ ion in forsterite host coherent qubit operations robust against thermal decoherence up to 10 K?

Before

Prior non-Kramers Fe2+ qubits (Smoleński et al.) required deliberately engineered lattice-mismatch epitaxial strain in CdSe/ZnSe quantum dots to induce degeneracy, demonstrated only spin-state characterization and optical readout, and had no coherent gate-control mechanism.

But

Theoretical simulation only; spin-phonon coupling constant GE is unmeasured; Raman and Orbach relaxation rates omitted because prefactors CR and AO are unknown; readout methods require lower temperatures than 10 K.

Tools

spin Hamiltonian diagonalization · time-dependent master equation simulation · surface acoustic wave (SAW) strain driving · Qiskit cross-validation

Abstract

Quantum Computing uses quantum mechanical phenomena, such as superposition and entanglement of quantum bits (qubits), to represent and manipulate information in multidimensional state spaces. This approach allows complex mathematical functions to be executed simultaneously rather than sequentially, making them much more efficient than classical computers. However, current quantum computers suffer from quantum decoherence, where small changes to their environment, such as thermal fluctuations and vibrations, affect the systems' fragile states. The goal of this study is to discuss the functionality of a proposed Fe²⁺:forsterite qubit system by solving the unitary time-evolution of a quantum state vector for the system's Hamiltonian, using known axial and traverse anisotropy terms at temperatures up to 10 K. The system can effectively transfer population between its two lowest states at rates predicted by the Rabi half-period, with 99.9% fidelity. Additionally, it can hold the population at a desired state without docohering. The results remained consistent for temperatures up to 10 K, meaning, unlike many common qubit systems, the proposed qubit system could function without a dilution fridge and is not fragile to thermal noise.

item.title: Collective Superconducting-Qubit Interfaces for Microwave-to-Optical Quantum Transduction
item.description:
Worth a look theory — Collective coupling near half-excitation k=N/2 scales nearly linearly with N, speeding excitation transfer, but relaxation from the additional excited qubits offsets the gain. Mechanical anharmonicity of 100kHz raises single-photon target probability from 19.6% to 99.7% for N=4 qubits, while pair-dependent qubit-qubit interactions degrade optical retrieval efficiency from 58% to 35%.

Grade 0.426 · 1.8σ above the day's baseline · matched “Charge-insensitive qubit design derived from the Cooper pair box” · Nicolas Dirnegger, Matthew Guibord, William Munizzi, Chee Wei Wong, Prineha Narang

Figure

State populations over time during transfer from |D24,0m,0o⟩, showing suppression of multi-phonon leakage and boost in target single-photon probability with 100kHz mechanical anharmonicity.

Asks

Can a collective superconducting qubit ensemble coupled to a mechanical intermediary overcome weak electromechanical coupling to improve microwave-to-optical quantum transduction?

But

Theoretical model and master-equation simulations; assumes identical transmons and prescribed heating power-laws from optomechanical crystals.

Tools

Tavis-Cummings collective Dicke model · Auxiliary transmon Kerr-blockade · Input-output linear Langevin equations · Master equation simulation with disorder and noise

Abstract

Microwave-to-optical quantum transduction is essential for connecting superconducting quantum processors through optical networks. Mechanically mediated transducers, however, remain limited by weak electromechanical coupling, dissipation, and added noise. In this work, we study a transducer in which an ensemble of superconducting qubits couples collectively to a shared optomechanical resonator. For weak signals, we show that ensemble size and optical pump strength together set the conversion efficiency, added noise, and bandwidth, with pump heating limiting efficiency to a finite optimal pump strength. Near half excitation, the collective coupling grows nearly linearly with ensemble size, accelerating transfer of an excitation into the mechanics. We show that this speedup is offset by relaxation of the additional excited qubits, so the single-qubit coupling and lifetime still set the coherence requirement. Transferring exactly one excitation also requires an anharmonic mechanical mode, which an auxiliary qubit coupled to the mechanics can provide. In a lossless prescribed-Kerr benchmark with four qubits and g_sm/(2π)=3.81 kHz, a mechanical anharmonicity of 100 kHz raises the final joint single-photon intracavity target probability from 19.6% to 99.7%. Finally, we quantify the effects of decoherence, disorder, residual qubit--qubit interactions, and pump-induced qubit noise, finding that pair-dependent interactions reduce the optical retrieval efficiency from 58% to 35%. These results establish the coherence and selectivity requirements for collective quantum transduction.

item.title: Dressed-State Quantum Information Processing Using a Multilayer Ion Trap Chip with an Integrated Radio Frequency Resonator
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Multilayer ion trap with integrated 12.64 GHz spiral resonator drives bare 171Yb+ hyperfine transitions at Ω=1.2300(27) MHz with 10 mW input RF. Demonstrates individual addressing of two dressed-state qubits spaced by 10 μm using amplitude modulation, achieving a dressed Rabi frequency of 3.165(24) kHz on the target ion while crosstalk excitation on the adjacent ion is unresolvable (expected ≤0.4%).

Grade 0.420 · 1.7σ above the day's baseline · matched “Semiconductor spin qubits” · Ivan A. Boldin, Elham Esteki, Bogdan Okhrimenko, Friederike Giebel, Konstantin Thronberens, Amado Bautista-Salvador, Christian Ospelkaus, Christof Wunderlich

Figure

Excitation probability versus pulse duration for two 171Yb+ ions separated by 10 μm driven by a single amplitude-modulated RF field. Top panel shows resonant Rabi oscillations at 3.165(24) kHz in the addressed ion; bottom panel shows the adjacent spectator ion remaining in its ground dressed state due to a 43 kHz detuning from the axial RF gradient.

Asks

Can an on-chip integrated RF resonator produce an axial magnetic field amplitude gradient sufficient to individually address and manipulate dressed-state trapped-ion qubits without nulling the field at ion positions?

But

Demonstrated on a two-ion Coulomb crystal; multi-qubit entangling gates not yet implemented; input RF line exhibited 7.4 dB losses before the chip-carrier.

Tools

Multilayer microfabricated planar surface ion trap · Integrated RF spiral resonator · Trapped ¹⁷¹Yb⁺ ions · RF amplitude modulation

Abstract

We present the experimental preparation of a radio frequency (RF)-dressed-state qubit, the coherent operation of a single RF-dressed qubit, and the selective readout of RF-dressed hyperfine states of ¹⁷¹Yb⁺ ions trapped using a novel microstructured ion trap chip. We demonstrate the individual addressing of RF-dressed-state qubits in a two-ion Coulomb crystal. To this end, we developed, manufactured, and characterized a trap chip specifcally designed for quantum information processing with RF-dressed-state qubits. The chip consists of multiple layers, one of which includes an integrated resonator that creates a gradient of the RF magnetic field amplitude along the axis of a linear ion crystal. This RF gradient enables the individual addressing of dressed qubit states as well as their coupling. We characterize the ion trap chip experimentally using the hyperfine states of the electronic ground state of laser cooled ¹⁷¹Yb⁺ ions and by applying a single, global, modulated RF field oscillating near 12.6 GHz that drives dressed-state resonances. We present a microfabricated multilayer ion trap chip specifically designed for quantum information processing based on dressed-state qubits. This ion trap chip consists of multiple layers, one of which includes an integrated radio frequency (RF) resonator, creating a gradient of the RF magnetic field amplitude that allows for individual qubit addressing and qubit-qubit coupling. We experimentally characterize this ion trap chip demonstrating dressed-qubit state preparation, coherent single dressed-qubit operation, and dressed-state-selective read-out using hyperfine states of the electronic ground state of ¹⁷¹Yb⁺. For this purpose, a global modulated RF driving field oscillating near 12.6 GHz is applied to the ions. In addition, we demonstrate individual addressing of dressed-state qubits in a two-ion Coulomb crystal.

item.title: In-memory measurement-device-independent quantum key distribution
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Memory-assisted MDI-QKD protocol via in-memory matter-photon interference halves the required quantum memories and detectors, scaling secret key rate as O(η) and surpassing memoryless benchmarks at shorter distances.

Grade 0.416 · 1.7σ above the day's baseline · matched “Circuit quantum electrodynamics” · Nicolas Gauriot, Samuel Morrissey, Paul M. Burdekin, Ilse Maillette de Buy Wenniger, Sarah E. Thomas, Ian A. Walmsley, Robert I. Woodward, R. Mark Stevenson

Figure

Secret key rate plotted against total transmission distance for memoryless, dual-memory, and single in-memory MDI-QKD protocols across memory efficiencies of 25%, 50%, 75%, and 100%.

Asks

Can quantum memory-assisted MDI-QKD be simplified and improved by interfering a stored matter qubit directly with a travelling photonic qubit in a single memory?

Before

Two-memory assisted MDI-QKD requires two separate memories and double the detector count, with interference performed on a conventional beamsplitter after retrieving both photons.

But

Simulations assume symmetric links and asymptotic regimes without finite-size effects. Memory lifetime of telecom-ORCA must exceed several nanoseconds via rephasing or hyperfine control to beat memoryless links.

Tools

In-memory matter-photon interference · Dual-rail atomic ensemble quantum memory · Telecom-wavelength ORCA memory · Decoy-state MDI-QKD modeling

Abstract

Quantum memories offer to significantly extend the performance of quantum networks, but their complexity and limited performance at telecommunication wavelengths have so far hindered practical deployment. We propose a new memory-assisted measurement device independent quantum key distribution (MDI-QKD) protocol based on in-memory interference. Our approach leverages progress in atomic ensemble memories that enable the interference of a stationary matter qubit and a travelling photonic qubit inside a single quantum memory. We quantitatively evaluate the performance of this scheme against memoryless MDI-QKD and existing two-memory architectures, showing that it not only achieves superior secret key rates and surpasses the memoryless bound at substantially shorter distances, but also reduces hardware requirements by halving the number of memories and detectors. Our results further indicate that off resonant cascaded absorption (ORCA) memories are a particularly promising platform for implementing this protocol, and we outline a concrete design compatible with their capabilities. These findings demonstrate that in-memory interference provides a higher performance, and resource efficient route toward near term memory enhanced quantum secure communications.

item.arxave:abstract: Quantum memories offer to significantly extend the performance of quantum networks, but their complexity and limited performance at telecommunication wavelengths have so far hindered practical deployment. We propose a new memory-assisted measurement device independent quantum key distribution (MDI-QKD) protocol based on in-memory interference. Our approach leverages progress in atomic ensemble memories that enable the interference of a stationary matter qubit and a travelling photonic qubit inside a single quantum memory. We quantitatively evaluate the performance of this scheme against memoryless MDI-QKD and existing two-memory architectures, showing that it not only achieves superior secret key rates and surpasses the memoryless bound at substantially shorter distances, but also reduces hardware requirements by halving the number of memories and detectors. Our results further indicate that off resonant cascaded absorption (ORCA) memories are a particularly promising platform for implementing this protocol, and we outline a concrete design compatible with their capabilities. These findings demonstrate that in-memory interference provides a higher performance, and resource efficient route toward near term memory enhanced quantum secure communications.

item.title: Compute Before You Digitize: ADC-less Mixed-Signal Processing for Scalable Cryogenic Qubit Readout
item.description:
Worth a look new result — DIRAC eliminates Nyquist-rate ADCs via analog demodulation and ping-pong integration, using 50.3 pJ per qubit per readout (31.6× below fixed-point and 238× below FP32). Total 4 K quantum-classical interface power drops to 0.85 mW per physical qubit, a 50.4% reduction versus fixed-point digital baseband.

Grade 0.410 · 1.6σ above the day's baseline · matched “Superconducting Qubits: Current State of Play” · Qirui Zhang, Ben Toby, He Wang, Benjamin Lienhard, David Blaauw, Dennis Sylvester

Figure

Stacked bars of 4 K quantum-classical interface power per physical qubit (mW) broken down by subsystem across FP32, fixed-point, and DIRAC implementations, along with room-temperature flex and coaxial cable heat comparisons.

Asks

Can an in-cryostat readout receiver combine frequency-multiplexed qubit readout with neural network discrimination while reducing 4 K power below room-temperature cable loads?

Before

Conventional cryo-CMOS fixed-point digital baseband with 500 MS/s ADCs consumed 1.59 nJ per qubit burst energy (1.71 mW total 4 K power per physical qubit), saving only 36.7% power over room-temperature electronics with flex cables.

But

Evaluated on 1.12M experimental shots via behavioral models validated against transistor-level simulations over ten mismatch-sampled chips. Requires transmitter/receiver co-design with access to baseband NCO sign bits.

Tools

passive complex mixers · ping-pong active-RC integrators · voltage-to-pulse time-to-digital converters · TX-derived local oscillator reuse · joint matched-filter and neural network training · 22 nm FD-SOI cryo-CMOS at 4 K

Abstract

We introduce DIRAC, an ADC-less in-cryostat qubit readout architecture that uses analog computing to redraw the analog-digital boundary. Directly operating on the front-end's analog output, passive complex mixers perform the equivalent of digital demodulation, ping-pong active-RC integrators average their outputs into down-sampled per-qubit traces, and a time-domain stage digitizes them, eliminating Nyquist-rate ADCs. A TX-RX co-design derives the mixers' local oscillators from the readout transmitter's baseband rather than per-tone PLLs. A per-line calibration flow trains the matched filter jointly with the neural network, improving fidelity and enabling low-bit-width, low-voltage digital processing. Designed in 22 nm FD-SOI and evaluated at 4 K on 1.12M experimental shots, DIRAC matches the fidelity of a floating-point (FP32) digital pipeline for readout windows down to 750 ns, at 31.6× and 238× lower energy than the fixed-point (FxP) and FP32 pipelines. It cuts the total 4 K power per physical qubit by 50.4% and 68.6% relative to FxP and room-temperature flex cables, respectively. At a fixed logical-qubit count and 4 K budget, this yields, against FxP, a code distance larger by 2 to 6 and a 1.6-7.3× (Willow) and 4.9-204× (SI1000, p = 10⁻³) lower logical error rate.

item.title: QuFrame: Pauli Frame Tracking for Fault-Tolerant Quantum Control
item.description:
Worth a look new method — QuFrame closes the QEC feedback loop within a 1 µs round budget with fallback decoding in 144 ns, cutting the logical error rate by an average of 38.5% compared to a serialized blocking baseline.

Grade 0.408 · 1.6σ above the day's baseline · matched “Superconducting Qubits: Current State of Play” · Aleksandra Świerkowska, Ilgaz Er, Emmanouil Giortamis, Pramod Bhatotia

Figure

Logical error rate versus physical error rate scaling factor for a rotated surface code (d=3, 9 rounds). QuFrame avoids stalling and tracks closest to the ideal zero-latency baseline, outperforming the serialized blocking controller across all noise levels.

Asks

How can a quantum controller track the Pauli frame in real time with bounded per-instruction latency under multi-core dispatch and decoders of variable latency?

Before

A serialized blocking controller, as modeled in XQsim (Byun et al., 2022), increased logical error rates by up to 4.1× over an ideal zero-latency controller.

But

Evaluated on a distance-3 rotated surface code with 17 physical qubits; IBM Heron coherence times prolonged 10× in simulations; fallback lookup table memory scales poorly for higher code distances without truncation.

Tools

QuFrameISA · Instruction Resolution Engine (IRE) · Pauli Frame Management Unit (versioned compare-and-swap) · AMD Alveo V80 FPGA · Helios simulator with IBM Heron noise model

Abstract

Fault-tolerant quantum computing requires continuous quantum error correction (QEC) to suppress physical noise. While Clifford-only workloads can defer corrections to software post-processing, universal computation breaks this paradigm: executing non-Clifford gates via magic-state gadgets introduces hard, real-time control-flow dependencies on error-corrected measurements. Consequently, the controller must extract syndromes, decode them, and update the Pauli frame in real time, closing the entire QEC loop within a strict 1 μs cycle. However, prior proposals on Pauli frame tracking remain largely theoretical, leaving the microarchitectural bottlenecks of tracking, resolving, and synchronizing frame updates across distributed control pipelines unaddressed. To this end, we present QuFrame, a control microarchitecture for real-time Pauli frame tracking that closes the QEC loop within 1 μs while sustaining QPU-rate throughput. By introducing QuFrameISA, we cleanly decouple instruction execution from continuous Pauli frame management. Execution is distributed across per-qubit Instruction Resolution Engines (IREs) that resolve instructions against the frame via a single table lookup, while a Pauli Frame Management Unit enables independent, lock-free concurrent commits. To strictly guarantee the 1 μs deadline, QuFrame pairs an asynchronous primary decoder with an on-chip fallback decoder that resolves in 144 ns, natively reconciling divergent updates in hardware without degrading logical error rates.
